newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks more China rights concessions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks more China rights concessions.

text.p: The United States welcomed on Thursday a possible Chinese concession on human rights but said it still planned to seek a U.N. resolution condemning Beijing's record next month in the absence of more progress.

If China signed two key U.N. human-rights pacts, "That would be a positive step forward, but there are other very important measures that would need to be taken to indicate that there has been a fundamental change in Chinese government positions here," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

In Beijing, the Chinese foreign ministry said earlier in the day that it was "actively considering" signing the human-rights covenants which would give the international community a right to keep tabs on its performance.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang, asked if China would sign the covenants, said: "We are actively considering this," a repetition of what China has said since the mid-1980s.

He added that it would remain up to Beijing to decide when to ratify the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and a similar document on economic, social and cultural rights. Together the pacts would obligate China not only to uphold freedom of speech, assembly and religious worship, but also to report to U.N. monitoring bodies.

White House spokesman Michael McCurry said that if China were to sign, the United States would take that into consideration in deciding whether to try to censure China at the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

"We would consider that development in connection with any action in Geneva," he said. "But our concerns about human rights would certainly continue and would certainly continue to be an aspect of our presentations as we exchange views with the Chinese side."

The State Department later said the United States continued to consult its friends and allies about a resolution it plans to co-sponsor condemning China's rights record at the annual human rights conference in Geneva starting next month.
"We'll continue to do that because there's been no corresponding action by the Chinese government that would stop that process," Burns said.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said after visiting Beijing on Monday that, in the absence of Chinese concessions, the United States would co-sponsor the resolution. But she added there was "still time" to avert such a step if China acted to satisfy U.S. concerns.

China's statement of active consideration of signing is nothing new, according to Xiao Qiang, executive director of Human Rights in China, a New York group founded by Chinese students during the Tiananmen democracy movement crushed in 1989.
"It should not be considered as a change in China's attitude on this," he said, adding that China has said it was considering signing the pacts since the mid-1980s.
